title: Reversing Nodes in Groups of K

phrases.explanation: To rearrange elements directly within the existing structure without using extra storage
An unusual or extreme input scenario that may require special handling
To trace through the algorithm step by step using a concrete input
Changing the references or links between nodes in a data structure
The leftover nodes that do not form a complete group

technical_terms.definition: A linear data structure where each node points to the next node and the last node points to null
A placeholder node placed before the head to simplify edge case handling
A technique where a function calls itself to solve smaller subproblems
Reversing elements by modifying pointers directly without allocating a new structure

concept: Given the head of a singly linked list and an integer k, reverse every group of k consecutive nodes. If the number of remaining nodes is less than k, leave them in their original order. Return the modified list's head.

solutions.label: Extract to Array
solutions.summary: Copy all node values into an array, reverse each group of k in the array, then rebuild the linked list from the modified array.

solutions.label: Recursive Group Reversal
solutions.summary: Recursively reverse the first k nodes, then call the function on the remaining list and connect the results.

solutions.label: Iterative In-Place Reversal
solutions.summary: Use a dummy node and iteratively reverse each group of k nodes in place by manipulating pointers directly.

lines.speaker: interviewer
lines.text: You are given the head of a singly linked list and a positive integer k. Your task is to reverse every group of k consecutive nodes. If the last group has fewer than k nodes, leave those nodes as they are.

lines.speaker: candidate
lines.text: Just to confirm, for a list one, two, three, four, five with k equals three, I reverse the first three to get three, two, one, and then four and five stay unchanged since there are only two left. Is that correct?

lines.speaker: interviewer
lines.text: Exactly. And k is always a positive integer less than or equal to the length of the list. The list will have at least one node.

lines.speaker: candidate
lines.text: What if k equals one? Then no reversal happens and we return the list as is, right?

lines.speaker: interviewer
lines.text: Yes, that's a valid edge case. Also consider k equals the full length of the list, which means you reverse the entire list.

lines.speaker: candidate
lines.text: Got it. So I need to process the list in chunks of k, reverse each complete chunk, skip any incomplete remainder, and return the new head. Let me think about approaches.

lines.speaker: candidate
lines.text: The simplest approach is to extract all values into an array list. Then I reverse every consecutive group of k elements in that array. Finally, I rebuild the linked list from the modified array.

lines.speaker: interviewer
lines.text: Can you walk through the example? List one through five, k equals three.

lines.speaker: candidate
lines.text: Sure. I copy values into an array: one, two, three, four, five. I reverse the first three elements to get three, two, one. The remaining two elements stay. Then I build a new list: three, two, one, four, five.

lines.speaker: interviewer
lines.text: What are the time and space complexities?

lines.speaker: candidate
lines.text: Both are O of n. We traverse the list once to fill the array, reverse in linear time, and rebuild in another pass. The array takes O of n extra space. It works but we lose the benefit of linked list structure.

lines.speaker: candidate
lines.text: A better approach uses recursion. First, I check if there are at least k nodes. If so, I reverse the first k nodes, then recursively process the rest and attach the result to the tail of the reversed group.

lines.speaker: interviewer
lines.text: Walk me through the recursion with our example.

lines.speaker: candidate
lines.text: Starting with one, two, three, four, five and k equals three. I count three nodes, so I reverse one, two, three to get three, two, one. Node one is now the tail. I recurse on four, five. Since only two nodes remain, fewer than k, I return them unchanged. Then I connect one's next to four.

lines.speaker: interviewer
lines.text: What about the complexity?

lines.speaker: candidate
lines.text: Time is O of n since each node is visited once. Space is O of n divided by k for the recursion stack, since we make one recursive call per group. This is better than the array approach in space when k is large.

lines.speaker: candidate
lines.text: The optimal approach avoids both extra space and recursion. I create a dummy node pointing to the head. For each group, I first count k nodes ahead. If enough exist, I reverse them in place using pointer manipulation, then move to the next group.

lines.speaker: interviewer
lines.text: How does the in-place reversal work for one group?

lines.speaker: candidate
lines.text: I track the node before the group, called previous group end. For the first group, that is the dummy node. I repeatedly take the node after the current head and move it to the front of the group. After k minus one such moves, the group is reversed. Then previous group end advances to the old head, which is now the group's tail.

lines.speaker: interviewer
lines.text: And the complexity?

lines.speaker: candidate
lines.text: Time is O of n. We traverse each node at most twice, once for counting and once for reversing. Space is O of one since we only use a fixed number of pointers. This is the best we can achieve for this problem.

lines.speaker: interviewer
lines.text: Great work. You showed three approaches: extracting to an array, recursive group reversal, and iterative in-place reversal. Each improved on space usage while keeping linear time.

lines.speaker: candidate
lines.text: Yes. The key insight is that linked list problems reward careful pointer manipulation. The iterative approach with a dummy node handles all edge cases cleanly and achieves constant space, which is ideal for this problem.
